Otherwise, we wouldn't be having this conversation. Yes, it's going to cost trillions of dollars in investment. but we're the only part of the globe that can afford it. Hello and welcome to another episode of the Inspiring Industry Podcast, where we share our conversations with leaders from around the globe. I'm your host, Danielle Chan, and in this episode, we're taking a look at sustainability in the oil and gas industry. Obviously, it's an especially controversial topic as the industry is under huge pressure to evolve into a greener and more sustainable sector. But what does that mean? And what are the implications for an industry that has so many other sectors built on it? Well, there really isn't anyone better to discuss the topic than an expert in the field. And today we're honored to be discussing today's topic with Henrik Rasmussen, the Managing Director for the Americas at Topso. Henrik graduated from the University of Copenhagen in 1989 with a degree in chemical engineering before relocating to the States in 1991. He has worked at Holur Topso for over 32 years and has held many technical and management positions for all Topso's business units. His technical expertise covers ammonia, methanol and hydrogen plant industry, and specifically the redefining industry for both catalyst and technology. In the last few years, Henrik has been heavily involved in Topso's green and blue process technologies to produce renewable fuels, specifically green and blue ammonia, methanol and hydrogen. Since 2007, Henrik has been the Vice President of Catalyst and Technology, with responsibility for Topso's catalyst and licensed technology business for the US, Canada and the Caribbean. In early 2021, Henrik took on the role as Managing Director for the Americas and is responsible for Topso's business in North and South America. Topso, as I'm sure Henrik will share, is a leader in catalysis and process technology and pioneers hydroprocessing and emissions management. Although it was founded in Denmark, the business has grown to become a global advocate in and provider of technology and solutions for the energy transition. There is so much to unpack there. And fortunately, this isn't the first time I've had the pleasure of speaking with Henrik. He is an incredibly knowledgeable expert in the gas and energy industry. But with new legislation in place and Russia and Ukraine war having just reached its two year anniversary and of course, global pressure for businesses to go green. Can the industry keep up? Let's find out. Henrik, thank you so much for taking the time to speak with me today. We have we have so much to uncover and work through in this conversation. But I think to get the ball going, I'd love to know a little bit more about how you came to be in the energy and gas industry. I have such a broad overview of your career that started out with chemical engineering and you've kind of progressed through Topso as well. But what brought you into the industry? I worked for Topso in Copenhagen initially, transferred to the U.S. in 91, where I then did a lot of plant startups and ammonia plants and refineries. And then over time, I sort of took over management roles in different parts of Topso. And today I manage Topso's activities in the Americas. So how did I get into it? Well, it's sort of always been the interest of mine to be in energy. Chemistry interests me. Design and engineering interests me. pending_qa.q: What are the main misconceptions about renewable fuels and the energy transition that Topsoe addresses?
pending_qa.r: The biggest misconception is that renewable fuels will be the same cost as fossil fuels, which they are not. Another major misconception is that we're about to phase out oil and gas entirely. Without government mandates and incentives, renewable fuel projects simply will not happen because they are significantly more expensive than fossil alternatives.

pending_qa.q: What multiple pathways does Topsoe pursue for the energy transition instead of relying on a single solution?
pending_qa.r: Topsoe pursues several pathways including sustainable aviation fuel from fats, oils and greases; blue ammonia and blue hydrogen using natural gas with CO2 sequestration; green fuels and green ammonia from renewable electricity; and continued investment in more efficient fossil fuel catalysts. Each pathway comes at different times due to different stages of commercialization and scale, and all are needed because there is no single silver bullet solution.
